title: What's Permaculture All About?
summary: Josh and Chuck explore permaculture: its definition as conscious design of agriculturally productive systems with the diversity and resilience of natural ecosystems, its three ethics (care for earth, care for people, limits on population and consumption), and its origins with Bill Mollison and David Holmgren in Australia in 1978. They cover Holmgren's design principles (zones and sectors, integrate rather than segregate, multiple functions per element, biological resources, succession, diversity, energy efficiency), the forest garden/agroforestry idea, a Schumacher College plot study comparing permaculture and conventional gardening, criticisms of the movement (lack of scientific testing, Mollison's dogmatism, exotic plants), and Josh's own backyard permaculture project in Atlanta with a cistern and swale. The episode opens with a Think Spring playlist introduction and ends with listener mail from Gail about unpaid fashion internships.

segments.title: Think Spring playlist intro
segments.summary: Chuck introduces the episode as part of the Think Spring playlist, followed by the show's standard opening.

segments.title: Opening banter and New York shows
segments.summary: Hosts greet listeners and discuss their recent live shows in New York City and the upcoming sold-out Tuesday show.

segments.title: Charles C. Mann and sustainability debate
segments.summary: Chuck mentions an upcoming interview with Charles C. Mann and his book The Wizard and the Prophet about feeding ten billion people, framing the techno-optimist versus sustainability debate between Norman Borlaug and William Vogt.

segments.title: What permaculture is and sustainability vs. unsustainability
segments.summary: Josh reveals he is redoing his yards in Atlanta with a permaculture company. The hosts describe permaculture as design principles for sustainable food production, contrasting it with big modern monoculture agriculture and explaining what sustainable and unsustainable mean, including fertilizer runoff and algae blooms.

segments.title: Managing land versus passive use
segments.summary: Robert Lamb's river analogy is discussed: permaculture involves management of the land in a harmonious way rather than passive use or wild rewilding, illustrated by the dog-petting analogy.

segments.title: Origins: Mollison, Holmgren, and the 1978 coinage
segments.summary: The term permaculture was coined in 1978 in Australia by Bill Mollison and David Holmgren, combining permanent and agriculture. The hosts describe the three ethics and how Mollison and Holmgren split, with Mollison seen as dogmatic and Holmgren more pragmatic. Ancient farming practices like crop rotation and forest farming are cited as precedents.

segments.title: Permaculture in mainstream farming debate
segments.summary: The hosts discuss whether permaculture can feed the world or should be incorporated into conventional farming, and agree a happy medium is likely best.

segments.title: Ad break
segments.summary: Short sponsor or break segment before the hosts return.

segments.title: Defining permaculture and the three ethics
segments.summary: The hosts read a widely circulated definition of permaculture and go through the three ethics: care for earth, care for people (including access to clean water as a right), and setting limits on population and consumption.

segments.title: Zones and sectors design
segments.summary: Josh explains zone-based design, with the most attended areas nearest the center and activity decreasing outward. Chuck describes sectors as pizza slices radiating from the center, overlaid on zones, based on observing sun, wind, water, and animals over a year.

segments.title: Relative location and integrate rather than segregate
segments.summary: Relative location is discussed with the example of placing crops downhill from a pond to avoid pumps. Holmgren's principle of integrate rather than segregate is cited.

segments.title: Multiple functions, redundancy, and diversity
segments.summary: A pond can provide irrigation, livestock water, and a barrier, and hedges serve as wind blocks. Diversification provides backups against losses such as avian flu, and the hosts tell an egg-basket joke.

segments.title: Energy efficiency and biological pest control
segments.summary: Energy-efficient design such as windbreaks is covered. Mollison's saying 'you don't have a snail problem, you have a duck problem' is discussed, along with using pigs or chickens to till and rotate crops. Buying lab-raised ladybugs is criticized as risking parasites for native populations; planting sunflowers to attract native ladybugs is suggested.

segments.title: Plant succession and nutrient recycling
segments.summary: Plant succession from barren land to weeds, shrubs, and forest is described, along with nutrient recycling through composting, with a reference to the earlier composting episode.

segments.title: Break
segments.summary: Short break between segments.

segments.title: Beth Stagg's Schumacher College plot study
segments.summary: Beth Stagg, a professor at Schumacher College in the UK, compared permaculture plots with conventional gardening plots. Conventional gardening yielded 13 kilograms of edible food per 100 square meters versus 2.3 kilograms for permaculture, but permaculture required far less time and input, and it held up better in a bad weather year over a three-year study.

segments.title: Yield debate and adherents
segments.summary: The hosts discuss whether permaculture can out-yield conventional farming and note that some adherents make strong claims, while the broader goal is not necessarily maximum yield.

segments.title: Forest gardens and agroforestry
segments.summary: A forest garden is a food garden built to imitate a natural forest, with tree, shrub, vine, and ground layers. Chuck notes agroforestry as an ancient technique, possibly from South America. Josh contrasts lawns with forest gardens.

segments.title: Josh's Atlanta backyard permaculture redesign
segments.summary: Josh describes a permaculture company owner's redesign of his Atlanta yard, which uses existing trees, native plants, and placement based on sun and wind. A roughly 500-gallon cistern under the deck collects roof runoff and feeds underground pipes and pumps for watering.

segments.title: Swales and groundcover
segments.summary: Josh describes the swale in his back corner yard, a level ditch with a berm that slows water so it soaks into the ground. Overflow from the cistern feeds it. Groundcover or mulch is planned instead of grass.

segments.title: Criticisms of permaculture and Mollison's exotic plants
segments.summary: Criticisms include lack of rigorous scientific testing and Mollison's stance on exotic plants, which contradicts the native-plant approach of the hosts' designer. Mollison's response is that ecosystems are already damaged and management is needed.

segments.title: Listener mail: unpaid fashion internships
segments.summary: Gail writes about her unpaid fashion design internship in New York, the expectation of an all-black wardrobe, and how unpaid internships contribute to a lack of diversity in the fashion industry.

segments.title: Outro and contact info
segments.summary: Chuck gives social media and email contact information and the website, and the episode ends.
